items.title: GCMDiff: a condition-guided diffusion framework for pharmacophore-fragment drug discovery and target-specific molecular design
items.abstract: Drug discovery remains a costly and time-consuming process, motivating the development of artificial intelligence approaches to accelerate molecular design. Many generative models, including generative pre-trained transformers (GPT), rely on one-dimensional SMILES representations that lack explicit structural topology and are constrained by rigid syntax rules. Moreover, most existing models perform unconditional molecule generation, while the few conditional diffusion approaches often rely on abstract parameters rather than pharmacologically interpretable constraints. Consequently, current methods have limited ability to enforce explicit drug-like and pharmacophore requirements during molecular generation. Here, we propose GCMDiff, a multi-condition guided diffusion framework for molecular graph generation that supports controllable and interpretable molecular design. Unlike SMILES-based models, GCMDiff employs an atom-pair and bond-centric molecular graph representation that directly captures explicit chemical topologies. Crucially, we introduce an interpretable pharmacological condition embedding that integrates multi-modal constraints, including atom number, Lipinski’s Rule of Five constraints, and structural moieties derived from Checkmol, PubChem, and Rings in Drugs descriptors. These explicit features guide the diffusion process toward promising chemical spaces satisfying user-defined prerequisites. Benchmark experiments demonstrate that GCMDiff generates chemically valid and structurally diverse molecules, achieving 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while maintaining atom and bond distributions consistent with drug-like chemical space. As a practical application, GCMDiff was applied to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor design, where generated candidates reproduced key binding interactions, including the conserved hydrogen bond between a quinazoline scaffold and residue Met793. These results demonstrate that GCMDiff provides a flexible and interpretable framework for pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation, enabling controllable exploration of drug-like chemical space and facilitating early-stage rational drug discovery. Scientific contribution GCMDiff advances molecular design by employing a graph-based diffusion framework that bypasses SMILES-related syntax limitations. Its core innovation is a multi-modal condition encoder integrating drug-like properties and pharmacophores, enabling interpretable, pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation. The model achieves 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while demonstrating practical utility through the design of novel EGFR inhibitors that replicate essential Met793 binding interactions. This framework effectively bridges generative AI with rational, constraint-driven lead optimization.

items.abstract: The article addresses the topical issue of using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in working with academic texts by combining practical work with GenAI, the analysis of dissertation abstracts, and the development of students’ critical attitudes toward AI-generated information. This study investigates the ability of generative artificial intelligence to reconstruct selected conceptual components of academic discourse without direct access to the corresponding dissertation abstract. The study analyzes contemporary scholarly approaches to the use of generative artificial intelligence in academic discourse. The aim of the study is to empirically determine the extent to which GenAI can reproduce the relevance, research aim, and research focus of an academic study based on a minimal set of input data. The methodology involved an experimental procedure with 25 undergraduate students enrolled in the program “Language and Literature (German). Translation” within the field of Germanic languages and literatures. The empirical material comprised 25 abstracts of successfully defended dissertations on Germanic linguistics. Two generative AI systems, ChatGPT and Gemini, were used in the experiment. Following a standardized prompting procedure, the systems were provided with the research topic, but the corresponding dissertation abstract was not made available to them. The AI-generated responses were compared with the corresponding conceptual components of the dissertation abstracts using comparative content analysis. The results indicate that GenAI can semantically reconstruct selected characteristics of an existing academic study, including its relevance, research aim, and focus. At the same time, the findings do not indicate textual copying of dissertation abstracts but rather suggest the possibility of reconstructing their content-related characteristics from limited input data. These results indicate the considerable potential of GenAI as a tool for supporting academic writing. Practical implications. The findings may be used to develop university curricula that establish a balanced approach to integrating generative artificial intelligence into the educational process while preserving fundamental principles of academic integrity and values.

items.title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
items.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI AND THE RESHAPING OF SECOND LANGUAGE WRITING: A COGNITIVE PROCESS PERSPECTIVE
items.abstract: Addressing how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes the cognitive act of second language (L2) writing, this conceptual article draws on recent empirical literature (2023–2026). It grounds its analysis in the Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (CPTW), chosen because its decomposition of planning, translating, and reviewing under working-memory limits illuminates how cognitive labor is redistributed between learner and machine. Through CPTW, three key insights emerge. First, planning undergoes an externalization of productive struggle: offloading idea generation causes learners to bypass essential rhetorical problem framing. Second, translating experiences a voice constraint: model optimization toward conventionality flattens non-standard L2 syntax and homogenizes authorial voice. Third, reviewing suffers a reviewing bifurcation, splitting evaluation into goal-level appraisal and opaque decision-level monitoring. Theoretically, GenAI transforms writing into a co-generative sociotechnical practice requiring GenAI feedback literacy. Pedagogically, educators should adopt process-oriented assessments, using pre-prompting framing logs, annotated drafts, and prompt histories to evaluate cognitive engagement over polished final products.

items.title: Generative AI as a Co-Creator in Innovation Management
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping innovation management by moving beyond its conventional role as a technological tool toward becoming an active participant in creative and decision-making processes. This chapter examines how GenAI can function as a co-creator across the innovation process and explores the complementary roles of human and artificial intelligence in generating meaningful innovation outcomes. Adopting a structured integrative literature review approach, the study synthesizes recent research on GenAI-enabled innovation through thematic analysis and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate that GenAI contributes across multiple stages of innovation, including opportunity recognition, idea generation and evaluation, product and service development, business model innovation, commercialization, and organizational innovation. Its primary strengths lie in rapid content generation, knowledge synthesis, recombination, scenario development, and iterative refinement, whereas human contributors remain central to problem framing, contextual interpretation, strategic and ethical judgment, validation, and accountability. Building on these complementary capabilities, the chapter proposes the Human–GenAI Innovation Co-Creation Framework, which conceptualizes innovation as an iterative cycle of framing, generating, evaluating, refining, validating, and experimenting. The analysis further identifies hallucination, bias and idea homogenization, intellectual property concerns, human over-reliance, AI literacy, and organizational governance as important boundary conditions shaping the effectiveness of co-creation. Overall, the chapter argues that the transformative potential of GenAI in innovation management lies not in replacing human innovators but in designing organizational processes that deliberately combine human judgment and creativity with GenAI’s generative and synthetic capabilities.

items.title: Generative AI as Metacognitive Scaffolding in Undergraduate Mathematics: A Quasi-Experimental Study of Problem-Solving Performance and Engagement
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve university students’ mathematical problem-solving when it is designed not as an answer generator but as a metacognitive scaffold. Building on sociocultural scaffolding, self-regulated learning, and Pólya’s problem-solving model, the study tested a 15-week structured GenAI-supported intervention in Calculus I. A cluster-assigned quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 128 undergraduates distributed across four tutorial sections: two sections used a Socratic GenAI protocol (n = 60), and two sections received traditional instruction using the same weekly problem sets (n = 68). Students’ solutions were scored with a validated analytic rubric aligned with the four Pólya stages, and outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA with pre-test adjustment and a multilevel sensitivity model for section-level clustering. Results showed a statistically significant adjusted between-group difference favoring the GenAI-supported group, F(1, 125) = 28.76, p < .001, partial eta squared = .187, with the largest stage-specific effects for carrying out the plan and understanding the problem. Student perceptions were highly positive, and cognitive engagement showed the strongest association with performance gains. The study contributes to educational psychology by specifying a testable instructional mechanism: structured GenAI-supported instruction may support mathematical problem solving when prompts elicit planning, monitoring, explanation, and reflection while discouraging direct solution-seeking.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and terminology work: structural associations of prompt strategy preference, cognitive load, and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Introduction The widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in knowledge-intensive domains requires continuous adjustment of human cognitive patterns. In terminology work, aligning strict semantic standards against the non-deterministic output of large language models (LLMs) is closely intertwined with workers' subjective cognitive load. This study examines the structural associations among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, while testing the potential moderating role of professional experience. Methods Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1,760 practitioners using LLMs for terminology tasks, structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) were employed. SEM evaluated the linear structural associations among prompt strategy preference, self-efficacy, and cognitive load, while LPA identified behavioral user profiles. Multi-group equivalence testing was further conducted across three career stages (novices, intermediates, and experts). Results Prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with subjective cognitive load, with AI interaction self-efficacy serving as a significant mediator in this structural relationship. LPA identified three distinct user profiles (low, medium, and high strategy use), with the high strategy group exhibiting the lowest cognitive load and highest self-efficacy. Multi-group equivalence tests indicated no statistically significant moderation across experience cohorts, demonstrating structural invariance of the core model across career stages. Discussion From the perspective of cognitive ergonomics, upfront prompt structuring is structurally linked to downstream cognitive offloading and psychological buffering. These findings provide empirical evidence for individual cognitive resilience during human-AI collaboration in the generative AI era.

items.title: GeoPROV: A Semantic Provenance Profile for Coastal EO-Derived Products Informed by a Systematic Review of Spatial Data Supply Chains
items.abstract: Emerging remote sensing technologies increasingly support coastal observation through Earth observation (EO) derivatives such as satellite-derived shorelines, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)- and light detection and ranging (LiDAR)-based elevation models, coastal land-use/land-cover products, bathymetric grids, turbidity and chlorophyll-a indicators, habitat maps, flood extents, and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated segmentation outputs. These EO-derived products are central to shoreline monitoring, coastal vulnerability assessment, flood-response planning, marine ecosystem management, and land–sea administration. Yet their evidential value depends on transparent provenance: users must know which sensor, acquisition condition, preprocessing chain, algorithm, model version, validation dataset, and uncertainty estimate produced each coastal product. The review synthesises 156 eligible publications identified through a systematic review process. Of these, 89 studies containing sufficient implementation and methodological detail were selected for detailed analytical coding. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol, the review analyses application domains, provenance capture modes, representation strategies, semantic web technologies, and interoperability practices. The review identifies persistent gaps in feature-level lineage, alignment between the World Wide Web Consortium Provenance Ontology (PROV-O) and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) geospatial metadata standards, spatial semantics, AI workflow transparency, uncertainty traceability, and scalable querying. GeoPROV aligns PROV-O with ISO 19115/19157, GeoSPARQL, Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), and SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogue (STAC)-compatible catalogue practices. The framework enables EO-derived coastal products to be traced from raw observation through preprocessing, AI/geoprocessing, validation, catalogue publication, and coastal-administrative decision-making. The resulting GeoPROV profile integrates PROV-O, GeoSPARQL, SHACL, ISO 19115/19157 lineage concepts, and STAC metadata within a lightweight semantic framework demonstrated through a coastal EO product workflow and machine-actionable provenance implementation.

items.title: Global Burden, Temporal Trends, and Risk Factors of Low Back Pain Among People Aged 15–49 Years
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low back pain (LBP) remains a leading cause of disability worldwide. However, the disease burden among people aged 15-49 years has been insufficiently addressed. OBJECTIVE: The present study aimed to investigate the global burden, temporal trends, and attributable risk factors of low back pain among people aged 15-49 years. METHODS: Using data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study 2021, we analyzed the incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) of LBP across 204 countries and territories. Age-standardized rates (ASRs) were calculated, and temporal trends from 1990 to 2021 were examined using joinpoint regression. RESULTS: According to GBD 2021 estimates, there are approximately 16,993,809 new cases of LBP that occurred worldwide, with South Asia bearing the highest case load. Although ASRs of incidence (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.12), ASRs of prevalence (AAPC: -0.17; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.14), and ASRs of DALYs (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.18, -0.14) declined between 1990 and 2021, absolute case numbers and DALYs increased. Occupational ergonomic factors (28.4%, 95% CI: 26.3%-30.7%), tobacco smoking (11.4%, 95% CI: 7.6%-15.2%), and high body mass index (BMI) (10.9%, 95% CI: 1.1%-21.0%) were the major attributable risk factors. Women always bear a more severe disease burden than men, with the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) being 3788.64 vs. 2380.94 per 100,000; the age-standardized prevalence rate (ASPR) being 8822.52 vs. 5410.51 per 100,000; and the age-standardized DALY rates (ASDR) being 999.13 vs. 626.28 per 100,000 in women and men, respectively. When it comes to the socio-demographic index (SDI), ASIR and ASPR initially increased with rising SDI, reaching a peak in Australasia, with ASPR over 12,500 per 100,000 and ASIR over 5000 per 100,000, before subsequently decreasing with further SDI increments. CONCLUSIONS: Despite declining ASRs, the absolute global burden of LBP among individuals aged 15-49 continues to grow, particularly among women and in high-SDI regions. Targeted preventive strategies and control measures are urgently needed.

items.title: Governing AI-Assisted Board Decisions: A Dual-Lock Model for Information Independence and Accountability
items.abstract: Purpose: This study develops a governance architecture for board-governed strategic decisions in which artificial intelligence (AI) provides common advice while legal and organizational decision ownership remains human. It examines two linked risks: erosion of independent human information and distortion of delegation through outcome-dependent credit and blame. Methodology/Approach: A theoretical decision-economic model is used to formalize firm-optimal and executive-optimal delegation, an endogenous attribution wedge, common-AI-induced error covariance, and boundary conditions for pre-AI information recording. The analysis treats governance controls as ex-ante commitments rather than ex-post corrections. Findings: Common exposure to an imperfect AI signal can increase correlation among revised human judgments and reduce the effective number of independent checks. Separately, private attribution incentives can move delegation away from the firm-optimal benchmark. The proposed Information Lock records designated human assessments before common AI exposure, while the Accountability Lock fixes effective decision rights and attribution rules before outcomes are known. The model also identifies limits: perfectly reconstructible post-AI judgments reduce the Information Lock mainly to an auditability device, while residual career downside can shift distortion from over-delegation toward rejection or delay of positive-value decisions. Conclusion: The contribution is a unified, selective governance architecture linking information independence and outcome-invariant accountability. It provides boards and senior executives with an implementable framework for preserving informational diversity, clarifying decision ownership, and distinguishing poor process from unfavorable stochastic outcomes in AI-assisted strategic decisions.

items.title: Hopelessness among Healthcare Workers during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Experiences and Perceptions
items.abstract: Background: COVID-19 has globally challenged health systems and created profound psychosocial consequences for healthcare workers. Hopelessness, as a negative future expectation, may emerge alongside fear, anxiety, and burnout. This study aimed to examine hopelessness levels among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and to identify associated factors based on their experiences and perceptions.Methods: The research group consisted of all employees at an education and research hospital. Data were collected from 562 personnel (48.2% of active staff). The data collection tools included a questionnaire and the Beck Hopelessness Scale. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni/Tamhane post-hoc tests, and stepwise multiple linear regression model.Results: The mean age was 35.8±8.8 years, and the mean length of service was 9.1±8.3 years. Of the participants, 61.2% were female, 30.8% were doctors, and 27.0% nurses. Nearly one-third had worked in COVID-19 units, one-third had been infected, and more than half had directly cared for COVID-19 patients. In bivariate analyses, smoking, workplace reassignment, direct care of patients with COVID-19, and perceiving colleagues’ knowledge as insufficient were associated with higher hopelessness. In the multivariable model, female gender, chronic illness or disability, a mixed work schedule, psychological impact, the belief that the pandemic could not be controlled, and pessimistic expectations about returning to normal life remained independently associated with hopelessness.Conclusion: Hopelessness is a critical psychological concern among healthcare workers in pandemic disasters. Early recognition of vulnerable groups and institutional support to reduce uncertainty, provide adequate Personal Protective Equipment, and regulate shift work are essential to strengthen workforce resilience. These findings highlight the need to integrate psychological well-being into pandemic preparedness and occupational health policies.

items.title: How Artificial Intelligence Facilitates Sustainable Food Consumption: The Mediating Roles of Perceived Usefulness and Trust
items.abstract: Background As climate concerns intensify and artificial intelligence transforms retail experiences, understanding how AI tools influence sustainable consumption decisions has become increasingly critical. This study investigates how AI-assisted shopping affects consumer purchase intentions for plant-based proteins—a key lever for dietary sustainability—by examining the mediating roles of perceived usefulness and trust in AI technology. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, we propose that AI usage and environmental concern influence purchase intentions through dual cognitive and affective pathways. Method We test this framework using survey data from 519 Amazon customers in the United States, analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The measurement model demonstrates excellent psychometric properties, with all constructs exceeding recommended thresholds for reliability and validity. Results The study reveals that both AI usage and environmental concern significantly enhance perceived usefulness of AI for sustainability decisions and trust in AI recommendations, which subsequently drive plant-based protein purchase intentions. The effects operate entirely through these mediating mechanisms, with perceived usefulness showing stronger influence than trust. The model explains 22.4% of variance in purchase intentions, indicating substantial explanatory power for behavioral research. These findings advance theoretical understanding of AI-mediated sustainable consumption while offering practical guidance for e-commerce platforms and marketers. Conclusions The study demonstrates that digital technologies can facilitate environmental behavior change when consumers perceive them as both useful for achieving sustainability goals and trustworthy in their recommendations, particularly among environmentally conscious consumers.

items.title: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) Challenge Linguistics?
items.abstract: Geoffrey Hinton — often called the "Godfather of Artificial Intelligence" — has openly criticized Noam Chomsky, raising profound questions about the relationship between linguistics and artificial intelligence. This paper examines four dimensions along which large language models challenge established linguistic paradigms. First, should linguistics pursue a macro or micro-orientation? This debate concerns both the scope of linguistic inquiry and the transformation of its research methods; the paper argues that linguistics must shift from a narrow, discipline-confined perspective toward a comprehensive, interdisciplinary "macro-linguistics" that integrates with the humanities, natural sciences, medicine, and engineering, and that spans phonetics, grammar, semantics, and pragmatics. Second, are language and thought separable or inseparable? Contrary to the traditional dichotomy, this paper argues that human thought cannot be entirely separated from language: the primary purpose of thought is communication, and without new information, thought loses its vitality — artificial attempts to disconnect thought from communication are therefore counterproductive. Third, is language acquisition innate or experiential? Artificial intelligence has significantly challenged Chomsky's innateness hypothesis, abandoning the premise that language is a pre-programmed, innate ability in favor of treating language as fundamentally experiential — a shift validated by the landmark successes of experience-based learning models. Fourth, can AI possess thought, or even constitute life? The paper argues that artificial intelligence cannot possess life in the biological sense: AI's language is fundamentally disconnected from genuine thought, linguistic fluency does not equate to autonomous thinking, and AI remains an incomplete imitation of human language and cognition rather than an autonomous thinking entity.

items.title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/PrivacyTrace.

items.title: How university social responsibility shapes staff citizenship behavior: a theory synthesis for teaching, research, and student support
items.abstract: Universities depend on staff contributions that exceed formal duties, such as sharing teaching practices, supporting students beyond scheduled hours, and volunteering for curriculum and quality-assurance work, to sustain teaching, research, and student support. University social responsibility (USR) is enacted largely through these same staff. Yet it remains unclear when staff perceptions of USR strengthen such discretionary contributions and when they are experienced as additional, unrecognized demands. This theory-synthesis article integrates USR, micro-level corporate social responsibility, organizational behavior, and recent higher education research to explain how perceived USR may translate into organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) among academic and administrative staff. Two pathways are proposed. A relational pathway links perceived USR to organizational justice, grounded in workload allocation, teaching assignments, promotion, and participation in decisions, and then to organizational trust, work engagement, and OCB. A motivational pathway links perceived USR to intrinsic motivation, engagement, and OCB when responsibility-related academic activities support autonomy and competence. Perceived organizational support is proposed to strengthen the relationship between perceived USR and organizational trust. Eight numbered propositions (P1-P8) are developed; Proposition 7 contains two constituent serial pathways (P7a and P7b). OCB is differentiated by its target: colleagues, students, and the institution. The framework identifies professional autonomy, collegial norms, role type, and workload systems as conditions that shape these relationships. Implications concern aligning USR commitments with fair academic workload, supportive practices, and recognized voluntary collaboration that benefits teaching and the learning environment.

items.title: Human Centered AI Ethics, Algorithmic Bias, and Data Synthesis in Social Work and Military Settings
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the ethical and professional implications of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical and community Social Work and its application within military settings, focusing on algorithmic bias, AI assisted data synthesis, privacy, and the preservation of human judgment. Research Methodology: The study adopts a qualitative documentary research design that draws on peer reviewed literature, professional standards, international policy documents, and relevant national frameworks. The documents were analyzed thematically through the lenses of Human Centered Design Theory, Sociotechnical Systems Theory, and the Social Justice Perspective. Results: AI offers opportunities to improve assessment, documentation, psychosocial intervention, research, and organizational decision making, but it raises serious concerns about privacy, confidentiality, informed consent, accountability, algorithmic bias, and transparency. These concerns intensify in military settings, where AI systems may process highly sensitive personal, health, and operational information about personnel, veterans, and their families. Conclusions: AI should be treated as a professional support technology rather than a substitute for Social Work judgment, therapeutic relationships, or accountable institutional decision making. Responsible adoption requires institutional safeguards, professional competencies, continuous auditing, meaningful human oversight, and mechanisms through which affected people can challenge AI supported decisions. Limitations: The study relies on secondary documents, does not test specific AI systems empirically, and focuses mainly on the Nigerian policy context. Contributions: The study proposes a Human Centered AI Framework for Social Work and Military Practice (HCAI SWMP) built on ethical governance, bias aware data management, secure data synthesis, and human centered implementation.

items.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

items.title: Human or Machine? EFL Students’ Trust Calibration in AI-Generated English Content:A Study at the Faculty of Languages, Surman
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university EFL students for language learning and academic tasks, yet fluent output may be inaccurate. This study examined self-reported trust and verification practices and students’ judgments of selected AI-generated English content among undergraduates at the Faculty of Languages, Surman, University of Sabratha. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was applied to questionnaire responses from 38 students. The instrument included background questions, ten five-point Likert items, five evaluation tasks with confidence and verification-intention responses, and an optional open-ended item. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Spearman’s rank correlations were used. Mean self-reported trust was 3.36/5 and verification was 3.74/5. Students correctly judged 62.1% of task responses under the primary answer key. Use frequency was not significantly associated with trust (ρ = .279, p = .090), whereas verification was associated with accuracy (ρ = .473, p = .003), as was confidence (ρ = .648, p < .001). Findings are preliminary given the small sample, modest trust-scale internal consistency, and ambiguity in one evaluation item. In exploratory HC3 regression, confidence remained associated with accuracy (β = .51, p = .005), while reported verification did not uniquely reach p < .05 after confidence was included (p = .063). After Holm correction across 28 exploratory pairs, only confidence–accuracy and awareness–adaptive-trust correlations remained significant. The study highlights the value of teaching verification and interpreting trust relative to output reliability.

items.title: Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence for Socio-Emotional Learning in Autism: A Pedagogical Framework for Guided Interaction and Educational Responsibility
items.abstract: The progressive integration of artificial intelligence into educational contexts is reshaping approaches to instructional mediation, the personalisation of learning pathways, and interaction with students. These potential applications are particularly relevant within the field of social and emotional learning (Goleman, 2011), especially for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), for whom structured and predictable learning environments characterised by gradual progression may foster the development of emotional and relational competencies. However, the use of generative artificial intelligence systems requires careful consideration of the implications associated with content reliability, process transparency, and the attribution of educational responsibility (Floridi, 2022). Indeed, the fluency and apparent plausibility of AI-generated responses do not guarantee their accuracy. Human supervision and validation processes are therefore essential to ensure that the content produced is scientifically grounded, pedagogically appropriate, and consistent with the intended learning objectives. items.title: Human-led, AI-enabled: preventing another AI winter through workforce transformation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has played a role in life sciences research and healthcare delivery for decades, though its nature and applications have changed with each new technology. As early as the 1950s, symbolic logic models provided clinical decision support: a form of deterministic AI encoded human knowledge as rules that an AI logic model could follow and implement (Nawaz et al., 2025). These early rule-based systems highlighted both the promise and limitations of symbolic AI. Subsequent periods of over-expectation followed by underdelivery contributed to recurring "AI winters" in which investment and enthusiasm declined.After 2010, computational and algorithmic developments led to machine learning (ML) and deep learning models. While these performed extremely well in some use cases (Habehh and Gohel, 2021), notably in biomedical research and image analysis, their use remained largely concentrated among technical experts and specialized applications. In the 2020s, large language models (LLMs) have rapidly changed the AI landscape in life sciences and medicine, and we are on the cusp of even faster evolutions, with state space models and active inference-based concepts that could lead to non-linear, novel leaps.The adoption of LLMs has been unlike that of any other modern technology. Most innovations, such as cars, mobile phones, and the internet, have taken years (between 1 year and 75 years) to reach adoption by 50 million users globally (Desjardins, 2018), whereas ChatGPT took only 5 days to achieve this. This unprecedented uptake leads to a paradigm shift in how we think about the users, use cases, and impact of a new technology. LLMs could change working practices in nearly every industry, to varying degrees. In their lead article, Guni et al. articulate the potential influence of LLMs in life sciences research and healthcare delivery (Guni et al. 2026). They review the rise and fall of AI applications in biomedical research and clinical decision support, and robustly discuss the elements needed for the current wave of AI to succeed. Specifically, they comment that "multidisciplinary effort (is needed) across several key domains: i) algorithmic science and architectures, ii) datasets, iii) processing power and efficiency, iv) infrastructure, v) human factors through codesign, and vi) interoperability with both legacy and modern healthcare systems." These efforts will require collaboration between clinicians, researchers, technologists, patients, ethicists, policymakers and others, and Guni et al. discuss a thorough breadth and depth of key topics. However, a seventh critical domain underlies all the others: the transformation of biomedical education and workforce development. Without a workforce capable of effectively leading AI systems, even the most sophisticated algorithms, datasets, and infrastructure will fail to deliver lasting impact, and we risk another AI winter.With respect to education, the widespread yet heterogenous use of LLMs by students and professors alike is challenging current pedagogy and assessment frameworks. In some cases, students are using LLMs to study or complete homework assignments, yet their professors lack expertise and are unprepared to alter their syllabus, homework, or exams (Lelescu et al 2025). In other cases, faculty are trying to integrate LLMs but are being met by significant resistance by students (Farinosi and Melchior, 2025). LLMs are also changing the day-to-day activities of our workforce, where adoption is similarly mixed and there is limited infrastructure to support broad, comprehensive workforce development. Many proposed educational responses focus primarily on the development of AI competencies across the continuum of learners and professionals. However, an exclusive focus on AI competencies introduces two related risks: "cognitive de-skilling", in which professionals gradually lose critical expertise and skills due to over-reliance on AI and "never-skilling", where the next generation of learners never fully develops foundational competencies because AI systems perform those tasks from the outset.Currently, health systems plan to measure the immediate augmented performance of AI tools in terms of clinical outcomes or immediate workflow efficiencies; we have yet to comprehensively measure their impact on retained competency or the longer-term implications of their use as a performance standard. Over the next 50 years, AI will likely become a critical part of many decision-making processes, training programs, and assessments done in clinical settings. However, if we never measure the retained competency of clinical staff to understand the impact of AI on long-term skill erosion, we could unintentionally introduce a critical system failure in the future. Clinicians who can no longer spot errors in AI tools or perform tasks when tools fail may put patients at risk and create a new type of AI winter-a systemic failure due to over-reliance on AI and lack of human competency. This AI winter would be extremely damaging to the practice of medicine in multiple ways: 1) direct risk to patients, 2) time to re-skill a generation of medical practitioners, and 3) lack of medical leaders with expertise to train the clinicians.Life sciences and healthcare are not the first knowledge-intensive domains to confront the challenge of maintaining human expertise as automation becomes increasingly capable. As commercial aviation systems evolved to automate key functions such as takeoff, landing, and navigation, concerns emerged that pilots were becoming overly reliant on automation, potentially eroding critical manual flying skills and reducing resilience when automated systems failed. Recognizing this risk, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a Safety Alert in 2017 (FAA, 2017) and further guidance in 2022 (FAA, 2022) to strengthen policies and training that preserved pilot proficiency in manual operations.This experience provides a compelling parallel to the adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support systems. In both aviation and healthcare, humans and technology function as components of a sociotechnical system (Trist, 1981), where safety depends on the effective interaction between people, processes, and tools. When technological capabilities advance without corresponding attention to human competencies, organizations risk losing the very redundancies that protect against failure. The FAA's approach demonstrates that successful integration of automation requires more than technical performance; it requires deliberate governance, training, monitoring, and ongoing investment in human expertise. Ultimately, the safety of any automated system depends not only on the technology itself, but also on how human competency is preserved and strengthened alongside it (Macnamara et al., 2024).In short, humans must be the redundancy when technology systems fail.To avoid creating a generation of professionals who cannot function effectively when AI systems are unavailable, unreliable, or incorrect, we need radical transformation in our education and workforce development frameworks to teach both AI competencies and domain-specific competencies in synchrony. We must develop these competency frameworks now to prepare the future workforce to thrive in an AI-enabled world.Perhaps the easier competency framework is that of AI competencies. For example, prompt engineering, AI literacy, validation and oversight, ethical and responsible use of AI, agentic AI, and the nature of human-AI collaborations are obvious topics that biomedical education for life sciences research and healthcare delivery must begin to learn. Many programs around the globe have begun offering didactic and practical-based educational programs to serve this need. Perhaps more challenging is the listing of domain-specific competencies. Not every fact that previous generations were expected to memorize will remain equally valuable in an AI-enabled environment. The challenge lies in determining which foundational knowledge remains essential for independent critical thinking and reasoning, and which tasks can appropriately be augmented by AI. Future domain-specific competency frameworks may place less emphasis on memorization and greater emphasis on reasoning, interpretation, critical evaluation, communication, judgement, and collaboration. Each domain needs to develop their list of domain-specific competencies and then design pedagogy, training, and learning assessment around these competencies, assuming that AI will be a partner for the learner. Neither AI competencies nor domain-specific competencies alone are sufficient; future professionals will require mastery of both.The goal should be to leverage AI to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of biomedical research and clinical practice, allowing humans to focus on uniquely human activities such as critical thinking, creativity, and interpersonal connection, rather than repetitive and mundane tasks.Our society has seen workforce transitions before, for example as result of the invention of electricity, the Industrial Revolution, and the emergence of the internet. For example, online streaming services have rendered many jobs unnecessary, such as cashiers in video rental or record stores, while creating thousands of jobs never imagined in the 1990s. Similarly, if the current AI era succeeds some workforce roles will vanish, but many new roles will emerge, some unimaginable today. Leaders, researchers, educators, and workforce members must proactively develop systems and frameworks that enable current and future generations to thrive with AI technology at their fingertips.The future of biomedical research and healthcare should not be defined by "humans in the loop", but by "humans in the lead". Our challenge is not simply to build more capable AI systems. It is to build educational and workforce development frameworks that preserve human expertise while enabling effective human-AI partnership, i.e., systems that are "human-led, AI-enabled." History suggests that AI winters occur when technological capabilities outpace the ability of institutions, professionals, and society to effectively adopt and sustain them. Workforce transformation may therefore be one of the most important safeguards against another cycle of overpromising and underdelivering. If we succeed, AI can become one of the most transformative technologies in the history of medicine. If we fail, another AI winter may be closer than we think.

items.title: Human, AI-generated, and hybrid corrective feedback in L2 argumentative writing
items.abstract: This quasi-experimental study investigated the differential effects of human teacher feedback (HTF), AI-generated feedback (AIGF), and hybrid feedback (HF) on learner engagement and argumentative writing quality among 120 undergraduate ESL students across an eight-week intervention. Engagement (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) was measured via a purpose-built questionnaire and revision-tracking logs; writing quality was scored on a five-dimension analytic rubric. Repeated-measures ANOVA and multiple regression showed that HF was associated with the greatest improvement in writing quality (η²p = .24), HTF with the highest proportion of higher-order revisions, and AIGF with the highest revision frequency. Hybrid feedback condition membership was the strongest predictor of writing-quality improvement, followed by cognitive engagement. These findings have implications for AI-integrated writing instruction in higher education.

items.title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
items.abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.

items.title: Impact of AI Technology Proliferation on Internet Security
items.abstract: This conference presentation examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) proliferation on internet security, cybersecurity practices, software engineering, and digital sovereignty. It considers both the defensive capabilities enabled by AI technologies and the emerging security risks associated with their widespread adoption. The presentation discusses how AI-based solutions can improve cyberattack detection, threat analysis, incident response, and vulnerability identification. At the same time, it highlights the growing potential for malicious applications, including automated malware generation, phishing, deepfakes, social engineering, and disinformation. Particular attention is devoted to security vulnerabilities in AI-driven and agentic systems, including prompt injection, jailbreaking, training data poisoning, goal hijacking, and context manipulation. The analysis addresses the risks associated with excessive system privileges, persistent access to external tools, non-deterministic behavior, and dependencies on untrusted information sources. Security mitigation approaches include static and dynamic application security testing, the principle of least privilege, zero-trust architectures, sandboxed execution, and input/output validation. The presentation also explores the implications of AI-assisted software development, emphasizing the necessity of comprehensive code review, testing, and validation. It identifies potential challenges associated with vibe coding, cognitive debt, declining opportunities for junior developers, and the erosion of organizational knowledge and technical expertise. Broader societal and regulatory considerations include digital sovereignty, technological dependencies, open-source alternatives, responsible AI governance, and emerging European initiatives supporting technological autonomy. The presentation concludes that artificial intelligence can become a strategic asset for cybersecurity when AI models are developed using high-quality data, deployed within appropriate security frameworks, and subjected to effective human oversight and governance.

items.title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
items.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

items.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
items.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.

items.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
items.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

items.title: Inclusive co-design and AI devices: a new paradigm of pedagogical mediation for schools
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within Italian educational contexts represents one of the most complex digital transitions of the contemporary world (Han et al., 2022; Hopcan et al., 2023). Following the pandemic experience and the lockdown, schools have witnessed a proliferation of training offers for teachers, both curricular and specialized in support, often characterized by huge efforts. In this scenario, AI cannot be reduced to a simple instrumental innovation; in fact, it requires a profound redefinition of educational design and professional roles. Abandoning an initial technooptimism, international research today requires a critical-reflective approach: integrating these technologies without analyzing their ethical assumptions risks amplifying existing inequalities. As a result, the distinction proposed in the literature between an AI used "instead of education", which replaces the relationship, and an AI used "for education", which acts in support of human pedagogical goals, becomes fundamental (Holmes et al., 2022). items.title: INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND LEARNING ANALYTICS ON THE PERFORMANCE OF POSTGRADUATE STUDENTS IN UNIVERSITIES IN CROSS RIVER STATE
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: This study investigated the influence of artificial intelligence and learning analytics on the performance of postgraduate students in universities in Cross River State, Nigeria. The study specifically examined the influence of artificial intelligence technologies, ethical implications of artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and ethical implications of learning analytics on postgraduate students’ learning. Four research questions and four null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study was conducted in public universities offering postgraduate programmes in Cross River State. A sample of 300 postgraduate students was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving purposive, stratified random, and proportionate sampling procedures. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled *Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics Influence Questionnaire (AILAIQ)*. The instrument was validated by three experts in Educational Technology and Measurement and Evaluation, while a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained using Cronbach’s Alpha. Data collected were analyzed using simple linear regression to answer the research questions, while regression t-test was used to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that artificial intelligence technologies had a significant positive influence on postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 6.7% of the variance in learning outcomes (R = .259, R² = .067, t = 5.132, p < .05). Ethical implications of artificial intelligence also had a significant influence, accounting for 13.3% of the variance (R = .365, R² = .133, t = 7.512, p < .05). Learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, although its contribution was relatively small, accounting for 1.2% of the variance (R = .109, R² = .012, t = 2.107, p = .036). Similarly, ethical implications of learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 7.9% of the variance (R = .282, R² = .079, t = 5.627, p < .05). Based on these findings, the study concluded that artificial intelligence and learning analytics, as well as the ethical conditions surrounding their use, significantly influence postgraduate students’ learning in universities in Cross River State. The study recommended, among others, that universities should strategically integrate AI and learning analytics into postgraduate education, develop clear ethical frameworks for their use, strengthen digital infrastructure, and provide adequate training for lecturers and students on the responsible and effective use of these technologies. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, learning analytics, ethical implications, postgraduate students, academic performance, universities, Cross River State.

items.title: Information rather than architecture: cross-learner attribution and clinician–model complementarity in CIN2+ risk prediction for women referred for colposcopy
items.abstract: Background Deep tabular models, including self-supervised and pretrained foundation models, are increasingly proposed for clinical risk prediction, but their value over conventional learners is rarely tested against matched controls, and their role relative to clinician judgement is seldom examined. Methods In a retrospective single-centre cohort of 879 women referred for colposcopy (242 CIN2+, 27.5%), 15 routinely recorded variables, including a clinician image-based assessment documented before histopathology, were modelled with ten model families under one fixed protocol (single fold assignment and seed, no tuning). Discrimination was compared by paired DeLong tests and bootstrap. Two analyses were pre-specified: exact Shapley attribution of discrimination to five clinical groups of variables in every model family, and a complementarity analysis asking whether routine data identify CIN2+ among women judged negative by the clinician. Frozen models were evaluated in a 103-case two-centre external cohort. Results Out-of-fold AUROC ranged from 0.726 to 0.761. No model outperformed logistic regression (AUROC 0.757; CatBoost −0.002, p = 0.860; TabPFN +0.004, p = 0.554), and three matched ablations of a self-supervised tabular Transformer were null (all p ≥ 0.096). Removing the clinician assessment lowered AUROC in all ten families (by 0.041 to 0.072; all p ≤ 0.008). Shapley attribution ranked five variable groups identically in every family (Kendall’s W = 1.00; permutation p < 0.001): the clinician assessment (39% to 50% of discrimination above chance), then cytology, HPV testing, colposcopic findings and demographic history. The clinician assessment alone had sensitivity 0.504 and specificity 0.882; 49.6% of CIN2+ occurred in clinician-negative women. Re-reviewing the 20% of clinician-negative women with the highest model risk identified 34.2% (95% CI 25.7–42.7%) of the missed CIN2+, against 20% expected at random, raising pathway sensitivity to 0.674 at specificity 0.733. External AUROC of logistic regression was 0.710. Conclusions On routine structured data from a colposcopy-referral population, and under a common protocol, model architecture did not determine performance; predictor information did. Retrospectively, routine data complemented the clinician modestly in clinician-negative women, rather than replacing clinical judgement. Claims that complex architectures improve clinical tabular prediction should be tested against logistic regression with paired uncertainty across repeated data splits.

items.title: Inhabiting the Algorithmic Pulse: Affective Digital Literacy and Critical Citizenship in the Era of the Fourth Revolution
items.abstract: In the age of the Fourth Revolution, understood not only as the convergence of cyber -physical systems and artificial intelligence but also as a mutation of human self-understanding, the sharp distinction between online and offline dissolves into a constitutively hybrid "onlife" condition. Digital environments do not merely transmit information: they orchestrate emotional states, modulate attention and construct reputational identities, acting upon a subjectivity solicited from within rather than repressed from without. Setting out from Asimov's short story Evidence and the figure of the "maimed master", the essay locates the true terrain of the educational challenge not in computational power but in empathy and affectivity. The risk is not that machines will become human, but that humanity will grow accustomed to a synthetic affectivity, devoid of the weight of the body and of the responsibility inherent in relationship. items.title: Innovation in Education: India's Emerging Model, Government Initiatives, Challenges and Solutions.
items.abstract: Abstract Education is undergoing a significant transformation in response to technological development, changing social conditions, emerging employment opportunities and the increasing demand for practical and skill-oriented learning. In this context, innovation in education has become an important area of discussion in India. Educational innovation, however, should not be understood merely as the introduction of computers, smart classrooms or artificial intelligence. It includes changes in teaching methods, curriculum, assessment, classroom interaction, institutional practices and the relationship between education and society. The present paper examines the changing nature of educational innovation in India with particular reference to school and higher education. It analyses India's policy direction under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and discusses initiatives such as PM SHRI Schools, Atal Tinkering Labs, Frontier Technology Labs, digital education platforms, experiential learning and technology-enabled higher education. The paper also examines evidence from UDISE+ and the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 to understand the realities of educational development, particularly in rural India. ASER 2024 provides evidence on enrolment, foundational learning and, for the first time at national scale, digital access, usage and skills among children aged 14–16. The paper argues that India's emerging model of educational innovation is gradually moving from a technology-centred approach towards a broader model involving experiential learning, creativity, problem-solving, digital literacy, vocational exposure, holistic assessment and community participation. At the same time, challenges such as the digital divide, infrastructure limitations, teacher preparedness, unequal access and the tension between innovative pedagogy and conventional assessment continue to affect implementation. The study concludes that educational innovation becomes meaningful only when technology, teachers, students, curriculum and local context work together to improve actual learning.

items.title: Innovations and Challenges in Smart-Textile Wearables for Postural Monitoring: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: In many work environments, professionals perform physically demanding routines involving repetitive movements and prolonged static postures, increasing exposure to biomechanical risk factors associated with work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs). Wearable technologies offer opportunities for continuous posture monitoring and real-time feedback, but their occupational deployment remains challenging due to limitations related to comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and integration with work clothing. This scoping review aims to synthesize and critically analyze the existing evidence on smart-textile-based wearable systems for occupational posture monitoring. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and CINAHL was conducted, identifying 566 records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 34 studies were included in the final synthesis. The included studies were analyzed according to wearable architectures, sensing technologies, data processing and posture recognition, user feedback mechanisms, and energy management strategies. Hybrid architectures combining textile-based sensors and inertial measurement units, together with machine learning and real-time feedback, emerged as promising approaches for continuous posture monitoring. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical or laboratory validation, with relatively small samples and limited long-term evaluation in real occupational environments. Five studies reported changes in posture or ergonomic behavior following the use of the technology, while no direct evidence of reductions in WRMSD incidence or severity was identified. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial technological potential for smart-textile-based posture monitoring, but current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical or occupational effectiveness in preventing WRMSDs. Future research should prioritize prospective, long-term validation involving larger and more diverse worker populations under real-world occupational conditions, while addressing comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and compatibility with occupational clothing and personal protective equipment.

items.title: Innovative language teacher education approaches integrating ai-assisted models
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence within educational environments is profoundly reshaping language teaching. Language teachers are increasingly expected to operate in digitally mediated environments and to integrate technological tools into their pedagogical practice (Godwin-Jones, 2022). Yet resistance remains widespread. Without adequate training that addresses both the technical and pedagogical dimensions of AI use, hesitation is a predictable and, in many respects, rational response. The literature confirms that resistance to AI adoption stems from a structural deficit: limited preparation, insufficient theoretical grounding, and the absence of models that connect technological tools to principled language pedagogy (Godwin-Jones, 2022; Kovačić & Bubaš, 2023). This challenge is particularly acute in LSP education, where language learning is inseparable from disciplinary discourse, professional communication, and context-sensitive language use. Specialized discourse cannot be reduced to automated linguistic processing, and teachers who lack a robust pedagogical framework struggle to evaluate what AI tools can and cannot do within their specific instructional contexts. items.title: Institutional Governance Authenticity and Student Responses to Artificial Intelligence Assessment Guidelines in Higher Education
items.abstract: Abstract Rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities worldwide to issue guidelines on student AI use in assessment. While existing research catalogues policy content and student misuse, little is known about how students perceive these guidelines and how such perceptions shape behaviour. This paper argues that current research treats guidelines as a binary intervention—present or absent—overlooking their psychological and institutional authenticity. Drawing on procedural justice and neutralisation theories, we contend that when guidelines are vague, invisible, unenforceable, and treated by academics as box-ticking exercises, they fail as integrity safeguards and may instead provide justifications for disingenuous AI use. We further argue that this pattern reflects institutional compulsions—legal, reputational, and competitive—that drive guideline issuance despite known limitations. We propose a research agenda centred on guideline authenticity and its effects on fairness perceptions, moral neutralisation, and compliance intentions, alongside perceptions of institutional motivation. A sequential mixed-methods design is outlined, drawing on UAE and UK contexts. The agenda aims to move institutional practice beyond symbolic policy-making toward genuinely embedded academic integrity cultures.

items.title: Instructional Emotion in the Age of Artificial Intelligence：Value, Alienation Risks, and Pathways for Reconstruction
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence in education raises questions about how emotional experience, relational care, and professional responsibility can be sustained in increasingly data-mediated teaching environments. This conceptual article examines instructional emotion as an interrelated configuration of teachers’ emotional engagement, students’ learning-related experiences, and the affective relationships through which teaching acquires meaning. Drawing on scholarship on achievement emotions, caring pedagogy, teacher–student relationships, and artificial intelligence in education, the article organizes its analysis around three value foundations: embodied human experience, relational connection, and teachers’ professional responsibility. It then identifies four potential forms of alienation arising when technological efficiency overrides educational judgment: procedural rigidity in teaching methods, emotional distance in interaction, the loss of affective meaning in content, and the reduction of assessment to measurable performance. Corresponding reconstruction pathways include emotionally adaptive instructional design, humanistic interaction, affective knowledge graphs, and emotionally responsive assessment. These pathways are guided by teacher judgment and bounded by consent, fairness, transparency, and human oversight. The framework distinguishes the interpretation of emotional evidence from claims to measure learners’ inner states directly. Its contribution is to connect educational values, potential risks, and pedagogical responses within a coherent conceptual structure. The proposed relationships remain open to empirical examination across educational settings.

items.title: Instructors’ Perceptions of Microsoft Teams Reading Progress in an Omani EFL Foundation Programme: Adoption, Challenges, and Institutional Feasibility
items.abstract: Oman’s digitisation priorities under Oman Vision 2040 encourage the integration of technology into teaching and learning. Little research examines instructors’ perceptions of Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) Reading Progress in Omani General Foundation Programme (GFP) contexts, particularly regarding its pedagogical value, ease of use, and implementation challenges. This mixed-methods pilot study explored instructors’ perceptions of Reading Progress in General English 2 (GE2), within the pre-degree GFP at the Preparatory Studies Centre (PSC), University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Oman. MS Teams Reading Progress is an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported tool designed to help students practice reading aloud, improve accuracy and fluency, and give instructors performance data. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study explored instructors’ perceptions of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions, and behavioural intention. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from three sources: a structured questionnaire (N = 10), two semi-structured interviews, and MS Teams usage logs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed thematically. The findings reveal a disconnect between teachers’ positive perceptions and willingness to continue using the tool and students’ limited engagement. Although instructors believed the tool could support reading fluency and accuracy, its use remained low, possibly due to the timing of the pilot, the absence of continuous assessment (CA), and limited time within the course plan. The findings indicate that wider implementation would benefit from early rollout, integration into course design, and CA weighting.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence With PPE: A Smart Boiler Suit Framework for Maritime Survey Applications
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Marine surveyors are routinely exposed to complex hazards, chemical, ergonomic, and physical, within dynamic environments such as ships and offshore platforms. Existing personal protective equipment (PPE) provides only basic safeguards and remains largely reactive. This paper proposes the design and conceptual architecture of an AI‐enhanced smart PPE boiler suit specifically optimized for marine and offshore class surveyors. The proposed system is envisioned to leverage embedded sensor networks, edge/cloud artificial intelligence analytics, and real‐time communications for continuous hazard detection, predictive risk mitigation, and streamlined survey workflows. We detail a proposed system architecture, outline pathways for functional prototyping, and critically examine anticipated challenges, establishing a robust roadmap for future multidisciplinary research and industry adoption. No physical prototype has been constructed at this stage; all scenarios and performance figures presented herein are theoretical and intended to guide future empirical validation.

items.title: Interdisciplinary evaluation of assistive technology
items.abstract: This white paper is the deliverable of work package 2.5 “Interdisciplinary evaluation protocols” (german: “Interdisziplinäre Evaluierungsprotokolle”) of the Center for Assistive Technologies Rhein-Ruhr (Zentrum Assistive Technologien Rhein-Ruhr, ZAT, see Wild-Wall et al. 2024). It addresses the evaluation of assistive technology (AT), which we define as any device, software, equipment, or system that enables people with disabilities, functional limitations or special needs to perform specific tasks. The purpose of evaluating AT is to assess, in a systematic and reproducible manner, how effectively it fulfills its intended function in close interplay with the human user(s). Because AT, by definition, interacts with people, its evaluation must account not only for technological performance but also for social and human factors. A meaningful and comprehensive evaluation therefore requires an interdisciplinary perspective, drawing on the methodological toolkits of multiple disciplines and approaches.

items.title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
items.abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.
